sentences.text: Them.
Good.
How are you?
This meeting is being recorded.
Hey Jason.
How you doing guys?
Who have we got there?
Matt and Jason, is it?
Yep.
Yes sir.
How's it going?
Yeah, all good, thank you.
All good.
So Nancy and I spoke last week, so I think.
Was it Jason booked, booked the call straight after you got the speaking gig.
So I don't know, I don't know.
A little bit of confusion because I, I said that I couldn't make the or.
I didn't know whether you were going to make the call two weeks ago, but Nancy and I did actually speak.
So.
But, but happy to, to do a, a re.
A rematch and see where everybody's at.
Thank you.
And I am checking with Katie to see if she's going to be able to join us as well.
I know she's back to back all day today, so she may be just hung up on another call.
It's been one of those days, hasn't it?
I've had about seven or eight calls back to back.
Just like it's only 9:30 here.
I'm already on my third.
I think everybody's back to work.
It's that first full week back, isn't it?
I think so, yeah.
But you're not surfing today, it looks like.
Back at the desk.
I've even shaped the beard down a little bit.
It was kind of wild, man.
See, I told you.
Remember me, the English guy?
You're right, you're right.
But we had a great chat, Nancy, and so I guess you knew that we were having a second call booked even if it was by accident.

Perhaps I did send you some options of how we could work together, but happy to sort of start at the beginning again for the sake of Jason and Matt and just maybe, maybe we could just sort of re tee it up and talk through the process.
But it would be good also to hear from you guys what your involvement is in the business.
Obviously I know a bit of the background and the sort of startup story about Zillow and that sort of thing, but yeah, be good to hear a bit more about you and then we can talk about the process.
So just to fill you in on who we are, we're Capital A group, we're an M and a advisory.
We work just in marketing services.

So all of our clients are either agencies, buying and selling or, or investors in agencies, private equity groups, private investors working usually on the buy side with those types of companies, helping them to acquire targets.
But we also have the platform agencies co, which is a marketplace for agency buyers and sellers to buy and sell agencies.
So, yeah, over to you, Jason or Matt, if you could give us a bit of detail on who you are and what you're interested in, I can fill in the details.
Sure.
I can go first.
So I'm Matt Kaminsky.
Jason and I are partners with Nancy and Katie and fellow co founders of our Mother Bear business here.
And we started a digital agency called strike two in October of 2019, so almost six years ago.
And Nancy and Katie, when they had originally started Kingston Marketing Group, were one of our very first clients where we did a rebranding on their agency and their shop was strategy and comms.
And I don't know if I'm telling you a story you've already heard, so sorry, but maybe it will be interesting from the other side of things if you have already heard the story, but.
So we were digital and creative, they were strategy and comms.
And we started partnering on a lot of projects where, for example, Nancy and her team would be doing a strategy project and then it would lead to creative execution.
And we worked together for a number of years.

And to make a long story very short, we eventually realized that it was a one plus one equals three situation, and we partnered officially and merged our agencies and created this new brand and have been Mother Bear now for a year.
Less than a year.
A year.
A year and a half.
Yeah.
Oh, Mother Bear for.
Yeah, Mother Bear has been less than a year, but we've been.
Yeah, we merged for over a year.
So, yeah, that brings us to where we're at now.
And personally, I lead our creative department in terms of what I do around here.
Okay, brilliant.
All right.
Yeah.
I'd heard a little bit of that from Nancy a few weeks ago, and.
Sorry to interrupt.
It looks like Katie's in the waiting room.
Oh, is she?
Let's have a look.
She's just popped in.
I don't think I've seen Katie's.
I know.
Katie's been on vacation, so sorry I'm late.
I was on with a client.
Classic.
Yeah, nice.
Nice to meet you as well.
We were just going over the.
The backstory again.
Just being reintroduced again.
I don't know what you know about us, Katie, but just to fill you in.
So we're an M and A advisory, working just with marketing agencies.
So that's our expertise.
And I'm sure Nancy's filled you in.
We spoke a couple of weeks ago when I had a huge beard and was under an umbrella in the rain.
She did.
It seems to be the thing we've got A massive rainbow over the valley in front of me as well.
Funnily enough, been raining.
But yeah, so happy to, to, to get you up to speed on, on the kind of work that we do and, and perhaps how we can help you.
So yeah, was just catching up on what everybody else does.
And so Katie, you're a partner in the, the business as well?
Yeah, that's right.
Yeah.
Okay, cool.
All right.
So Nancy, why don't you sort of tell me what, what you're thinking, what more you sort of would like to.

I think, you know, we're, we're talking to, you know, a few different people just to figure out kind of what the right next move would be in terms of, you know, who we might partner with and what our timing looks like, all of that fun stuff.
So I really would just love to give the opportunity to Matt and Katie and Jason to hear more about your process and ask whatever questions they have just so we can all kind of.
It's hard to get all of us on calls, so I'm kind of doing some of the preliminary conversations and then bringing these guys in to make sure.
The more founders, the worse it gets when you're trying to sell.
Exactly.
So yeah, I would love to.
Where everybody is.
So everybody's in a different point, aren't there?
And I think, Nancy, you're more thinking how you could step, maybe step back from the business sooner.
The people in the team that might want to take over and be more part of the leadership post acquisition as well.
So yeah, just on our process.
So we run a fairly tight.
Well, we've got a few different tiers that you can work with us, but we run a fairly tight six month process.
So the idea really is that we're trying to get the business sold within a six month period.
We've actually done a few businesses where we've actually sold on the exact six months from starting as well on the actual anniversary of the day.
So it's a, it's a pretty tight process.
The first two or three weeks is really getting to know the business and getting everything set up.

We do evaluation of the business, but also we're building out all of the marketing materials, teaser, the im, which is like a banker's pitch deck and the listing on agencies co. And then we're building a list of potential buyers as well.
So every client has their own sort of unique niches that they tend to be in.
So there is a different pool of buyers for, for every type of business.
But we have a mailing list of 20,000 signed up for Agencies co. We also have a CRM of 130,000 agencies which are mostly in the US, but some in the UK and Europe.
And the majority of our business is actually US based.
I'm based in the uk, but some of our team's based in the US as well.
And so we run the, like I say, pretty tight process.

We get everything ready to go to market and once we've got everything agreed with you guys, then we're pretty much just marketing the business to our own mailing list and you know, the researched list that we've built as well.
And then usually after about a two or three month process of us bringing in buyers and you guys meeting them, we tend to get an offer around sort of three, three month mark, sometimes four months.
But what we're looking to do is get three or four offers on the table at the same time so that we can leverage for the best price.
But always and particularly in this scenario where either you, Jason and Matt are looking to stay on long term, we're really looking for cultural fit.
So it always boils down to that, even if we've got a really good offer on the table.
So we want a few offers on the table at the same time.
You pick from the best one and then we go into what's called due diligence.
Once we have an loi, which is a letter of interest signed which just kind of agrees what the offer looks like.
But then we get into due diligence that usually lasts 30 to 60 days which includes negotiation of the contract as well.
And so overall end to end it's about six month process.
Sometimes it's much quicker than that and sometimes it can drag on for a few months, but that's basically how we work.
Any questions?
Sure.
Okay, that's, that's helpful I think.
You know, a big question for me or probably is since as you mentioned, Matt and I would probably stay on a little longer or you know, we own a bit less.
So it's like we'll get a smaller check so we'll have to work, you know, more.
So who, I guess who do you see us selling to in terms of the type of company and like in terms of why they'd want to buy us and what roles might look like once we're acquired?
Yeah, I mean you can never sort of guarantee how it is going to go down, but so there's obviously a few different ways we can attract buyers.

One way would be for us to go after the sorts of clients that you have already so if you're in particular niches around retail or, or pets or whatever it is, then we, we can look around that vertical.
So we'll be looking for agencies that have similar clients.

And the other way to go is looking for, for agencies usually much larger that do the same types of services, you know, so you're either looking for, for somebody who is in your, your niche, has similar clients but doesn't have your service, or somebody that does your service but doesn't have those types of clients.
And then beyond that is financial buyers.
So that would be investors that don't really care too much, but they just have a thesis that marketing agencies are a good thing to invest in.
And that also includes private equity as well.
So those are kind of like the main buyers.
And in terms of you guys staying on, not staying on, the way that it usually works is there's usually a percentage of the cash upfront when the deal gets closed.
It's usually, but again, you can never guarantee these things.
It's different in every circumstance.
But it's usually 50% upfront if the buyer is a private buyer and they're getting an SBA loan.
So they could have an agency already or they might just be looking to invest.
It can be more than that, 80 to 100% cash upfront.
And the founders need to get out of the business and they want to run it themselves.
That's kind of like the terms of an SBA loan.

But if it's another larger agency, you know, somebody who's doing a roll up or looking to merge like five or six different businesses before they sell it on in three, three years or so, they usually want the founders to stay in and run the business for about three years.
It can vary, but three years is kind of the standard.
So the standard is 50% cash upfront and a three year earn out.

So if you guys had agreed to stay and say Nancy was looking to get out after six to 12 months for, for instance, then yeah, obviously the, the responsibility falls with you guys to deliver the sort of financial targets over that period to make sure that everybody gets the earn out that they're expecting.
So there is a bit of.
Yeah, that makes sense.
And after the minimum period, people pretty much always leave.
Or do you see, have you made some deals where people are like, oh, I actually like, like it here and people stick around?
Yeah, so it, it's kind of a, a very mixed bag.
I mean there's, again, there's no real guarantees.
I would say more often than not that the acquirer Would like you to sort of step into the hold company or the larger business with more responsibility the longer that you're in it.
I don't think they always want people to leave.
I think the reality is that a lot of agency owners know that they can just do it again.
They can build another business from scratch over a three year period to five year period and just sell it again to another acquirer.
So quite often founders do leave after the three year ownouts being completed.
But that's not to say it's a rule.
A lot of people do find it more comfortable being part of a larger business where they don't have to stress about payroll every month.
So people do stay in the larger business as well.
We sold a business about five years ago and that seller was put immediately into the, into the board.
He had much smaller agency than the business that acquired him, but very experienced and it was events, events marketing and he's still there as part of the board after five years.
He could have left after two years.
So he's still there.
But yeah, it varies.
Andrew, I have a question for you.
So you established that you guys try to hit this sort of six month benchmark of when you make a deal by how do you or have you assessed our sale readiness?

Because I would imagine there's some discerning or discernment that you would want to take with who you partner with and that you wouldn't want to just say any $5 million agency is right to work with you guys.
You know, you guys would only want to play ball with someone who you think you could hit that six month target with.
So what's that process like for you?
How do you know we're a good agency to partner with?
Yeah, so that is a good question, but actually the answer is there's a buyer for every type of agency.
So we've worked with really tiny agencies that are basket cases and you wouldn't even think that they would get many buyers.
Actually they become quite attractive targets to buyers of a certain size.
So if you've got a small agency sub 1 million and it's just trundling along, if you're an agency and you're doing one one and a half million in revenue, they're actually quite an attractive target.
So there's good buyers for those types of businesses and then a business of your size.
Yeah, again, you know, if you're doing around 4 to 5 million, there is a big pool of buyers.

So even if the company was in trouble, there would still be, you know, very experienced Agency owners out there that would be interested and of course profitable businesses that are doing 5 million would put us in, was put us in a good place for private equity buyers.
They like to buy businesses that have a track record and are profitable.
They're not interested in buying businesses that are failing.

So you would, you would have two lots of buyers which would be your small, small to medium sized roll ups groups of, of agencies that are building inorganically by acquiring agency businesses plus private equity.
It would give you a really good pool as well as holding companies as well.
They tend to buy from about the 5 million in revenue upwards.
So it kind of puts us in the sweet spot where you guys are currently at actually.
So it's pretty much all of the different types of buyers are around this.
Type of agency and follow up question it.
So it kind of seems like we super simplification we partner up.
You know, we, we have some sort of discovery process with you and it's like you're going to come back with, with potential buyers.
So just we would need to obviously position the, the agency.
We need to get the story right.
And Mark.
For sure I guess the question is at our size even you know where we're at in such a sound spot from a business health perspective and we have a high percentage of retainer clients.
When you're under 10 million it feels like it's very founder dependent the success of the agency.
So how are these buyers determining that we're a good acquisition target and is there a.
On paper we look good but then they need to sort of chat with us and make sure that we're someone they want to buy.
Like what, what is the process like to get from you know, potential buyer to loi.
So yeah they, they do a certain amount of, of their, their own pre sort of due diligence before they, they put an LOI in.
I, I've got to say that very honestly because we work with a lot of buyers on the buy side as well that it can only take maybe two or three meetings for them to be ready to put in an offer.
A lot of it is financial.
So if the company is extremely stable and is profitable then really whatever we put into that IM is usually enough to get their juices flowing.
They get excited and then their next step is always look on the website.
If the website is shit then it's an absolute nightmare.
So we do encourage our clients to reboot their websites if they're, they're not looking exactly right but they'll take a look at the website.
They'll get excited about their work.
Obviously, if you've got a.
A deck of capabilities deck or you've got some case studies, they'll be looking through those and that will be.
That's probably enough for them to, to get a good match.
But.
But it's always chemistry, you know, for buyers as well.
They want to make sure there's a good team there and that they're excited to work with it.
I mean, it's, it's a.
Even the buying process is an emotional roller coaster for the buyers.
They want to get excited about.
It's a human story and yeah, that's all part of it.
So, yeah, I mean, I don't know if that answers you, but yeah, that's what they're looking for really, is to get.
So it doesn't usually take more than three.
Three meetings, I found, but it can drag on.

But quite often they'll put in an LOI at that point, and then due diligence is where they find out all of the boring stuff, you know, how you're doing the work and what your processes are and all of that.
Cool.
Okay, cool.
Well, it sounds like.

Sounds like there's probably a bunch of questions that we can keep answering as we go along, but really, like you said, the onboarding process is where we kind of uncover where you guys are at, what the business looks like and what the story is.
Really.
We want to go to market with a straight story.
So if you guys want to stay in or you want to get out early, it doesn't really matter.
It sometimes will affect pricing based on, you know, if everybody wanted to get out early, for instance, it would probably create a certain amount of risk for the buyers.
So that would mean that they would price it lower than if everybody wanted to stay for three years.
But we get the story straight and then when we go out to market, yeah, we're going to get a bunch of interest at the start.
I think with you guys, we'll probably get really strong interest.
And once that interest has started coming in, yeah, they're going to want to meet with you.
They're going to want more documents.
You know, everybody's got a different approach as well.
The buyers are all different.
Some want to know just financial stuff.
Others can't wait to.
To meet the founders and get excited about the business and the creative processes that they're involved in.
Yeah, that makes sense.
I have a question.
I don't know if you can answer this, but you have a lot more experience with this kind of stuff than we do.
As we're thinking about the right time to sell for us as a business.
Right.
Like, business isn't going very well.
It's very easy for me to be like, let's sell immediately and be done with.
And if business is going well, that's probably a good time to sell.
But also, like, business is good right now, and it sort of makes it easy to be like, well, we should just keep doing this because it's going well, or maybe we can get to six or seven.
But we also.
I don't want to be like, myopic.
Right.
All of a sudden things can turn.
So, like, as we're evaluating internally whether it's a good time to sell or if we're selling ourselves short, things like that.
What.
How would we evaluate that?
If you have any thoughts.
Yeah, again, that's a.
It's a complex and multifaceted question.
But what, what I really believe is when you are ready to sell, I think that's the time.
Because one way or another, it will all shake out in the process.
If, if you are, you know, if everything's running really well, then of course, yes, that from a, from a seller's point of view, that is the best time to sell.
It's better to sell before everybody gets angry and bored and frustrated and there's problems in the business.
It's better to go to market when everybody's feeling really great.
The business has got a year or two years of provable growth, and you've got processes in place that are easy to transfer to the buyers.
All of those things do contribute to it being an easier process.

But equally, if you are facing problems, everybody's tired or there are, I mean, for whatever Nancy's reasons are for wanting to take a step back once you're at that stage, hanging on for the sake of it, to try and get to the point when it's all going to be good and sunshine and rainbows.
There is no guarantee.
Agencies, more than almost any other type of business, is a roller coaster anyway at the best of times.
And so I think, like I said at the start, all agencies have buyers out there.
So if you're all thinking, how do we get to selling this business as soon as possible or over the next three years, then that's probably the right time to go.
If everybody is completely happy and really doesn't want to sell the business, then no point.
Just keep doing what you're doing and keep taking the money.
And somewhere in between all of that lies the same thing.
And actually selling when you're happy.
Etc.
But yeah, I would say generally, if you want to, if you want to sell, that's the best time to explore it.
It can only get worse if you want to get out.
Sure, that makes sense.
But yeah.
And I don't know exactly where you guys are.
Obviously me and Nancy had a bit of a, an in depth discussion of where you are with the business.
The business looks pretty solid.
The fact that you're like 85 retainers is really good.

That's something that is going to make the business worth more and it also secures those new owners, you know, knowing that you guys have been sat on retainers for a long period of time and you have a large percentage of retainers, that, that's good, you know, but until I get into the business, we wouldn't know exactly where the sort of sweet spot is for you guys to start, you know, for us to, to be selling you into and promoting which parts of the business sound exciting and it's going to get buyers excited.
So, so cool.
Thank you.
Okay.
All right, so look, Nancy, I gave you some options.
How close do you think you are for pulling the trigger?
And what sounds more exciting to you?
Are you looking to run the six month process and make sure, you know, we're there day, day in, day out, making sure we're nudging everything along, or is there a more casual approach?
We can obviously test the waters within the next couple of months and it is a really good window for us to test the waters.
But maybe, you know, you don't need a guarantee that we're going to get out in six months.
You just, where are you?
Yeah, I think, well, we, the four of us have some time together tomorrow to kind of regroup and have that conversation.
So if we can get back to you, you know, late, probably would be your Wednesday by the time we all meet.
So.

But yeah, I think we're, you know, we're at a stage where we're ready to kind of kick off a process and we just have to like put heads together and make sure we're on the same page on, you know, which one's the right one.
And the business is on fire right now.
So we've got to get in a good way.
Like four of us.
Yeah, in a good way.
Not a fire sale, not a dumpster fire.
I got you overwhelmingly positive right now.
So, so we've got to figure out kind of our capacity honestly to, to manage this process internally.
And so I think once you've had those discussions tomorrow, we'll, we'll be in a better position to answer your question.
But I love that you guys offer and I don't know if you guys all got a chance to look at the.
The two kind of options that I forwarded along, but I like that you have kind of two different options for us to choose from.
Did you watch Arjun's.
Arjun's video?
He's.
He's got an Australian accent, but he's actually from la.
Oh, my gosh.
Yes.
And so, yeah, we can.
We can huddle up tomorrow and let you know.
All right, let me know.
Yeah, just.
Just on that.
So the timeframe is six months that we like to shoot for.
But the funny thing is right before Christmas as well.
Some.
If we've got a buyer that's really engaged and they've got an LOI in the business or as well.
We've had this on multiple times where people are just like, we just need to get it done before the.
Before the end of the year as well.
So this, this last run at it before Christmas is the most exciting time because we do get deals closed, like ridiculously quickly.
That's funny because our business does the same thing.
Well, because the budgets run till the end of the year and.
Exactly.
Everyone's like, so they're like, we've got 10 million to spend.
We need to get rid of it today.
Exactly.
But even if that doesn't happen, you know, still we could get a process up and running and be out by April as well.
So, yeah, certainly a good time to get started, I would say.
Just don't end up in July or August.
Those two are the slow months.
Yeah.
Nobody wants to work in those months, I think especially this year.
It's funny, I feel like more than ever.
Yeah, nobody wanted to come back.
Like normally last week on Tuesday, we'd expect it to pick up, but it was just grinding all of our as well.
Nobody answering any emails.
So.
I know it's been.
Yeah, it's been.
I mean, we're busy, but it's like just getting a hold of clients has been tricky.
Everyone's been patchwork quilt of vacation.
I need to.
I need to hop because I have.
A meeting with a client board of directors.
But it was really good to meet you, Andrew.
I'll chase you on Thursday, then I'll give you a bit of time.
Let me know what you want to do and I'm happy to.
Will do.
All right, thanks.
Nice meeting you, Andrew.

summary.action_items:
**Nancy Poznoff**
Conduct internal team meeting with Matt, Katie, and Jason to discuss M&A process options and internal capacity for managing the sale process (25:32)

**Andy Day**
Follow up with Nancy on Thursday to receive team decision on proceeding with M&A process (28:42)
summary.overview:
- Andy Day from Capital A Group highlighted their expertise in M&A advisory for marketing services and the Agencies.co marketplace for agency transactions.
- Strike Two, founded in October 2019, merged with Kingston Marketing and subsequently with Mother Bear, enhancing their market positioning.
- Mother Bear's revenue of $4-5 million positions it favorably among small-to-medium roll-ups, private equity, and holding companies seeking acquisitions.
- The agency maintains a robust client base with 85% retainers, bolstering its value and appeal to potential buyers.
- Capital A Group executes a six-month M&A process, generating 3-4 offers around the three-month mark to assess cultural fit.
- Important health indicators like high retainer percentages and profitability can significantly improve an agency's marketability.
- The quality of the agency's website is critical, with poor performance being a dealbreaker for potential buyers.
- Current business performance is robust, creating optimal conditions for selling, especially with year-end budget pressures approaching.
- July and August are noted as slow months for M&A activity, making the pre-Christmas period ideal for accelerated deal closures.
- The Mother Bear team is evaluating internal capacity and options for the M&A process in their next scheduled meeting.
summary.short_summary: Andy Day from Capital A Group introduced the meeting, emphasizing their role in M&A advisory for marketing agencies, highlighting their expertise in the Agencies.co marketplace. Matt Kaminsky shared insights about Strike Two, its inception in 2019, and the merger with Kingston Marketing Group, establishing the foundation of Mother Bear. The meeting outlined the M&A process managed by Capital A Group, which spans approximately six months, including a thorough business evaluation and marketing strategy. Mother Bear's revenue of $4-5 million places it in a favorable position among various buyer categories, including private equity and service-focused buyers. The discussion also covered deal structures, emphasizing the importance of retainer clients to enhance business value, and concluded with insights on optimal timing for selling and next steps for the Mother Bear team.
